title: How I Help Learners Sound More Advanced Without Fancier Words
author: Cecilia Nobre
summary: English teacher Cecilia Nobre pushes back on the popular basic-versus-advanced vocabulary posts that treat words as rungs on a ladder. She argues that words such as sad, gutted, and devastated do different jobs, differing in strength, register, and context, so swapping in a fancier word can produce language that sounds odd. A Friends scene in which Joey over-uses a thesaurus illustrates how sophisticated vocabulary can make writing worse. The hidden assumptions that longer, rarer, and more formal words are better create an unhelpful hierarchy. She offers four practical moves: teach collocations and frames rather than synonyms, build register work into ordinary lessons, repeat speaking tasks after narrow targeted feedback, and recycle a small set of expressions across several lessons. The through line is that learners need control and choice, which come from depth and repeated use rather than endless novelty.
points: Vocabulary is not a ladder from basic to advanced, because words differ in intensity, register, and the social situations they fit.
Learners should be shown how a word behaves through collocations and contexts instead of being handed fancier synonyms as upgrades.
Register work, such as comparing several ways to disagree and asking who could say them and to whom, belongs in ordinary lessons.
After a short speaking task, give feedback on just two recurring problems and have learners repeat the task later so new language becomes available in real time.
Reusing the same eight to twelve expressions across listening, reading, speaking, and writing builds depth and retrieval better than constant new material.
quotes: Learners don’t just need more words. They need to know what those words are doing, how strong they are, what sort of situation they fit, who might say them and what effect they create.
I’m devastated” is much stronger than “I’m very sad”. “Insolent” doesn’t mean “rude, but with a higher CEFR level”.
I don’t rummage through my mental thesaurus for exhausted, fatigued or weary just to prove I have unlocked Advanced English™. The boring little word is often the best one.
If your main criterion is “use a fancier word”, you can end up with language that looks impressive on paper but sounds bizarre in context.
If a learner knows sad, don’t give them devastated as an upgrade. Show how each word behaves: absolutely devastated, devastated by the news, a bit upset, pretty gutted.
Advanced learners need control over appropriacy, not just a larger lexical range.
Advanced proficiency depends heavily on depth, retrieval and flexible use, so repeated contact usually beats endless novelty.
